summary: This is a domain class: a plain Java object whose job is to hold the data describing one room of a house — its name, length, and width. It keeps those three values private and exposes them through constructors, getter and setter methods, and a readable text form.

lines.text: The class is named after the real-world thing it models, which is the whole idea behind a domain class.
Fields are declared `private` so that no outside code can reach in and change them directly; access goes through the methods below instead.
Room dimensions can be fractional, such as 12.5 feet, so `double` is the right choice rather than `int`.
A no-argument constructor creates an empty Room whose fields you fill in later with the setters. Many Java tools and frameworks expect a class to offer one.

lines.text: This second constructor lets you build a fully populated Room in a single step, which is the more common way to use the class.
The parameter and the field share the name `name`, so `this.name` says explicitly "the field belonging to this object" while the bare `name` means the parameter.
A getter hands out the value of a private field. Reading goes through a method so the class stays in control of its own data.
A setter is the only way outside code can change the field, which gives you one place to add validation later if you need it.
This annotation tells the compiler you intend to replace a method inherited from `Object`; if you misspell the method name, compilation fails instead of silently doing nothing.
Every object inherits a `toString` that prints a meaningless hash code, so overriding it makes `System.out.println(room)` show the actual field values.
The escaped `\'` puts a literal single quote around the name, making it obvious in the output where the text value starts and ends.
